# Primary health care–oriented reforms: the political economy dynamics underlying health-system shifts across nine countries

**Authors:** Anuska Kalita; Kevin Croke; Erica Barbazza; Susan Sparkes; Leonard Cosmas; Mohamed Hassany; Arnoldas Jurgutis; Don Matheson; Abdon Mukalay wa Mukalay; Vishwanath Andy Partapsingh; Belgacem Sabri; Marcela Schenck; Shamsuzzoha Syed; Viroj Tangcharoensathien; Zhamin Yelgezekova; Suraya Dalil; Faraz Khalid

**Affiliations:** Department of Global Health and Population, Harvard T. H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, United States | World Health Organization, Geneva, Switzerland | WHO Country Office in Kenya, Nairobi, Kenya | Ministry of Health and Population, Cairo, Egypt | World Health Organization, Astana, Kazakhstan | Centre for Public Health Research, Massey University, Turitea, New Zealand | University of Lubumbashi, Lubumbashi, Democratic Republic of Congo | Pan American Health Organization/World Health Organization, Office for Barbados and the Eastern Caribbean Countries, Bridgetown, Barbados | Tunisian Association for Defending the Right to Health/People's Health Movement, Tunis, Tunisia | Universidad de la República, Montevideo, Uruguay | International Health Policy Program Foundation, Nonthaburi, Thailand

## Abstract

Using evidence from nine countries (Democratic Republic of Congo, Dominica, Egypt, Kazakhstan, Kenya, New Zealand, Thailand, Tunisia, and Uruguay), we analyze the political economy dynamics that emerged during implementation of primary health care (PHC)-oriented reforms. Across these cases, we identify 10 recurring health-system “shifts” toward stronger PHC orientation, which serve as a descriptive framework for examining the political economy challenges reformers faced and the strategies they used to navigate them. Primary data were collected from 356 participants through key informant interviews, focus groups, and expert consultations and were triangulated with document review. Using deductive mapping and inductive thematic analysis, we identify 10 PHC-focused health-system shifts present in some or all of the cases. These entailed shifts from: (i) short-term initiatives with limited scope to long-term, system-wide transformations; (ii) centralized control to devolved multilevel governance; (iii) hospital-centric resource allocation to strategic reallocations favoring primary care; (iv) physician-dominated care to multidisciplinary teams including non-physician providers; (v) siloed disease-focused services to integrated models of comprehensive care; (vi) peripheral, minimally regulated private sectors to their integration and actively state-stewarded participation; (vii) passive input-based budget allocations and provider payments to strategic purchasing; (viii) perceiving citizens as passive recipients of care to building active community engagement; (ix) ad hoc data collection to embedded learning and accountability; and (x) externally driven changes to local ownership for reforms. Reforms routinely triggered political economy dynamics—opposition from physicians, hospitals, specialists, and central bureaucracies; citizen skepticism; and capacity and patronage challenges under devolution. Strategies to address these included: high-level endorsement and passage of legislation; use of political and economic windows of opportunity; local capacity-building; decentralized autonomy; formal engagement with physician associations; regulated private sector participation; strategic purchasing to incentivize a PHC approach; strong data systems and assessments; community engagement; and locally grounded design with domestic capacity and financing. The paper underscores the value of anticipating political economy dynamics for designing and implementing PHC-oriented reforms.

- There is limited literature on the political economy of primary health care (PHC), especially on the dynamics that emerge during implementation of PHC reforms. This paper seeks to advance conceptual understanding and provide real-world insights into PHC-oriented health-system reforms through a political economy lens.

- Ten recurrent health-system “shifts” emerged in varying forms in the reform cases that we study, each provoking and being shaped by political economy dynamics. Distinct strategies were used by reformers to navigate these challenges.

- Policymakers should anticipate distributional conflicts and embed PHC policy changes in durable institutional reforms, pair financing and organizational changes with transitional support, prioritize community and public engagement, and leverage windows of political opportunity for sustained reform.

## Introduction

Primary health care (PHC) is defined by the World Health Organization (WHO) as a whole-of-society approach to optimize both the level and equitable distribution of health and well-being through three core components: primary care and essential public health functions as the backbone of integrated health services; multisectoral policy and action; and the empowerment of people and communities (WHO and UNICEF 1978, 2018a). There is growing evidence of PHC’s vital role as the foundation of a holistic approach to health-system strengthening (Starfield et al. 2005, Starfield 2012). Endorsed by many countries worldwide in the 1978 Alma-Ata Declaration (WHO and UNICEF 1978) and renewed in the 2018 Astana Declaration (WHO and UNICEF 2018b), there has been a resurgence of global commitment toward PHC as the cornerstone for achieving universal health coverage (WHO 2024).

Yet implementing the PHC approach in practice is both technically complex and deeply political. PHC-oriented reforms inherently involve redistributive processes that reallocate resources and decision-making power. Reforms that transform models of care, for example, require comprehensive changes that involve a range of stakeholders and address multiple core functions of the health system. These shifts can entail allocating more resources toward prevention rather than an exclusive focus on curative care, bringing services closer to where people live, and tackling the root causes of ill health by addressing upstream needs and social determinants. When pursued at scale, implementation of these reforms unfolds across the entire health system, entailing a complex set of challenges to vested interests. As a result, the political economy dynamics associated with PHC-oriented reforms often play a decisive role in shaping their feasibility, implementation trajectory, and sustainability.

Political economy analysis helps uncover the underlying politics of reform processes by examining the incentives, power dynamics, interests, behaviors, and constraints in a system and how they influence resource distribution, policy, and programmatic decisions over time. Despite widespread recognition of the centrality of politics to health-system reforms, these dynamics—with some notable exceptions (Bossert and Parker 1984, Cueto 2004, Croke 2021, Ashubwe et al. 2024, Croke and Ogbuoji 2024, Jurgutis et al. 2024, Matheson et al. 2024, Rajan et al. 2024, Schenck et al. 2024, Tangcharoensathien et al. 2024, WHO 2024)—remain underexplored in the literature on PHC. As a result, much of the existing literature, and associated policy guidance, often overlooks the political economy dynamics that underpin PHC-oriented health-system reforms.

To help address this gap, the WHO Special Programme on PHC launched the PHC Implementation Solutions Initiative (World Health Organization 2025), which aimed to document and share lessons from diverse country contexts on how PHC-oriented health-system reforms have been successfully implemented. As part of this effort, an initial set of nine country case studies was developed between 2022 and 2024, focusing on the political economy dynamics underpinning the implementation of PHC-oriented reforms. Each case study examined a specific PHC reform retrospectively over a defined period of time, analyzing the politics of its implementation. A subset of in-depth individual country case studies is published elsewhere (Cueto 2004, Ashubwe et al. 2024, Matheson et al. 2024, Schenck et al. 2024, Tangcharoensathien et al. 2024).

This study analyzes nine country case studies to examine the political economy dynamics associated with implementing PHC-oriented reforms. Through this analysis, we identify a set of recurring health-system “shifts” that may emerge when countries attempt to strengthen the PHC orientation of their health systems. These shifts provide a descriptive structure for examining how reforms redistribute resources, authority, and professional roles, and how these changes trigger political economy dynamics during implementation.

Rather than representing a linear reform pathway or a uniform reform package, the “health-system shifts” identified in this analysis should be understood as “ideal-type” directions of change synthesized from heterogeneous country experiences. Individual countries implemented different subsets of these shifts, and often to varying degrees. The purpose of identifying the shifts is, therefore, not to evaluate the completeness of reform in each country but to provide a comparative lens through which the political economy dynamics associated with PHC-oriented reforms can be examined.

Specifically, we address the following three research questions:

- What were the common health-system “shifts” toward PHC introduced across the country cases?

- What were the political economy dynamics resulting from these shifts?

- What strategies were used by reform actors to navigate these political economy dynamics?

## Materials and methods

### Sample and background on country cases

Our diverse sample comprised nine countries representing each of the six WHO regions—Dominica and Uruguay from the Americas region, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and Kenya from the African Region, Kazakhstan from the European Region, Thailand from the South-East Asian Region, New Zealand from the Western Pacific Region, and Egypt and Tunisia from the Eastern Mediterranean Region. These countries were purposively selected, based on having initiated significant PHC-oriented reforms. The sampling strategy was guided by expert consultation with WHO colleagues at global, regional, and country levels, and with national counterparts. For each country, a local team was set up to lead data collection and analysis. The respective teams selected specific reform(s) to serve as the focus of the analysis. The reforms examined in these case studies occurred across different time periods and political contexts, ranging from reforms initiated in the 1990s and early 2000s (e.g. New Zealand, Thailand, and Uruguay) to more recent PHC strengthening initiatives implemented in the 2010s and early 2020s (e.g. Kenya and Kazakhstan). The reforms also varied in scope and focus. Some involved system-wide health sector transformations aimed at strengthening the PHC orientation of the entire health system, while others focused on specific policy instruments or institutional reforms, such as decentralization of governance, expansion of multidisciplinary primary-care teams, strategic purchasing reforms, or new mechanisms for integrating private providers. Across the cases, reforms therefore encompassed a range of policy domains, including governance arrangements, health financing mechanisms, workforce policies, service delivery models, and community engagement mechanisms. ### Data collection

This study draws on data from multiple sources collected through a collaborative research process involving the local country teams. Each country team comprised domestic experts, including researchers, academics, civil society representatives, and government officials. Importantly, several members of each country team included policy actors who were directly involved in designing and implementing the respective PHC-oriented policies. First, we conducted a comprehensive review of both published and gray literature, as well as national policy, strategy, and guideline documents. These were identified through keyword searches using PubMed, Google, and Google Scholar, and through consultations with health policy experts in each country. Additionally, we accessed databases from WHO, the World Bank, and respective national governments to gather relevant information. Where necessary, documents published in local languages, reviewed by the country teams, were included to ensure a comprehensive understanding of each country’s PHC-oriented reform efforts.

Following the document review, we identified key stakeholders related to the selected PHC reforms. This process was informed by the policy documents and reports we reviewed and consultations with senior policy actors who had been directly involved in the reform processes in their respective countries. We collected primary data through stakeholder consultations, focus group discussions (FGDs), and semi-structured in-depth interviews with key informants representing various stakeholders in each country. These stakeholders included government officials, health-care providers, community representatives, and civil society members, among others. Informed consent was obtained from all study participants before their involvement, and, where permitted, interviews and FGDs were audio-recorded to ensure accuracy. The confidentiality of all participants was strictly maintained, and the local teams de-identified all data before sharing it with the study team.

In total, 356 respondents participated in the study between 2022 and 2024. This included 102 key informant interviews, 32 FGDs (each involving four to six participants), and four larger expert consultations, which included 10–25 participants per session. ### Data analysis

The data from the stakeholder interviews, FGDs, and consultations were analyzed using the Framework Method, which allows a combined approach to analysis, enabling themes to be developed both inductively from the accounts (experiences and views) of research participants and deductively from existing literature (Gale et al. 2013). We present the different analytical approaches we used in Table 3.

*Table 3 The different approaches used in the data analysis.*

| Stage of analysis | Analytical approach | What it applies to |
|---|---|---|
| Characterization of reforms and health-system shifts | Deductive | WHO PHC Operational Framework levers |
| Theoretical understanding of political economy dynamics in the PHC reforms | Deductive | Historical institutionalism (temporality, institutions, interests, and ideas) |
| Identification of specific political dynamics and strategies to navigate them | Inductive | Emerged from thematic analysis of interviews, FGDs, and consultations data |
| Cross-country synthesis | Inductive | Patterns across cases |

The WHO/United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) Operational Framework for PHC (WHO and UNICEF 2020) provided the deductive analytical foundation for this study. We used 14 strategic and operational levers (Fig. 1) to classify the entry points and design features of reforms across cases. We then synthesized these levers into 10 higher-order “health-system shifts” that represent recurring system-level directions of change toward stronger PHC orientation. Each shift corresponds to one or more of the Framework’s levers; the purpose of this synthesis was to provide a parsimonious comparative structure for examining how clusters of PHC levers—when pursued in practice—triggered political economy dynamics during implementation. Political economy dynamics and reform strategies were then identified through thematic analysis of interview/FGD/consultation data and triangulated with the document review.

*Figure 1: Operational framework for PHC theory of change. Source: WHO and UNICEF 2020.*

Next, we used inductive analysis to identify the political economy dynamics that emerged in each of the shifts, and the political strategies used by the policy actors to navigate these dynamics. The identification of the 10 health-system “shifts” served primarily as an organizing framework to examine how different types of reforms generated distinct political economy dynamics and reform strategies across countries. We categorized these political strategies based on the key themes that emerged from the analysis. The themes were validated by the country teams.

Our analysis also drew on historical institutionalist approaches to political economy, which emphasize how reforms unfold over time within specific institutional and political contexts. Drawing on this literature, particularly work by Thelen (1999) and Thelen and Mahoney (2015), we examined reform processes through four analytical dimensions: temporality, institutions, interests, and ideas. Temporality refers to how reform trajectories evolve over time and interact with political windows of opportunity. Institutions refer to the formal and informal rules that structure decision-making and governance arrangements. Interests capture the incentives and power dynamics among actors affected by reforms. Ideas refer to the framing of reform goals and policy paradigms that shape political support or opposition. These dimensions provided a conceptual lens for interpreting the political economy dynamics observed across the country cases.

In this paper, we present the analyses that triangulate findings from the primary data with those from the document review across all nine countries’ PHC reforms, and also draw upon the previously published country case studies (Ashubwe et al. 2024, Jurgutis et al. 2024, Matheson et al. 2024, Schenck et al. 2024, Tangcharoensathien et al. 2024).

## Results

Based on our deductive and inductive analyses, we identified 10 key shifts across our sampled countries to bring about a stronger PHC orientation to their health systems. These shifts are analytic groupings of the WHO/UNICEF PHC Operational Framework’s levers (Fig. 1), synthesized to describe system-level directions of change across heterogeneous reforms. While reforms in four out of the nine countries contained all 10 shifts (Kazakhstan, New Zealand, Thailand, and Uruguay), the shifts were not fully achieved even in these four countries. Therefore, these shifts represent the “ideal-type” description of the major health-system shifts identified across the sample. These comprise shifts from: (i) short-term initiatives with limited scope to long-term, health system–wide transformations; (ii) centralized control to devolved multilevel governance; (iii) hospital-centric resource allocation to strategic reallocations favoring primary care; (iv) physician-dominated care to multidisciplinary teams including non-physician providers; (v) siloed disease-focused services to integrated models of comprehensive care; (vi) peripheral, minimally regulated private sectors to greater integration, with active government stewardship; (vii) passive input-based provider payments to strategic purchasing; (viii) perceiving citizens as passive recipients of care to building active community engagement; (ix) ad-hoc data collection to embedded learning and accountability; and (x) externally driven changes to local ownership for reforms. Political economy dynamics emerged within each shift, and reform actors used various strategies to navigate these dynamics, with varying degrees of success. Table 4 lists the common health-system shifts, the corresponding levers from the WHO/UNICEF PHC Operational Framework, the political economy challenges associated with each shift, the strategies reformers used to address them, and illustrative examples from the country cases.

Across these shifts, several recurring political economy dynamics emerged. Most prominently, PHC-oriented reforms often generated resistance from actors whose resources, authority, or professional roles were affected—particularly physicians, hospital-based providers, and central bureaucracies. Reforms that redistributed resources or decision-making authority also produced tensions between national and subnational actors and triggered debates over fiscal autonomy and institutional control. In addition, reforms that expanded community participation or introduced new accountability mechanisms sometimes encountered resistance from administrators or political leaders wary of increased scrutiny. Reform actors employed a range of strategies to navigate these dynamics, including seeking high-level political endorsement, a phased approach to implementation, concurrent institutional reforms, stakeholder engagement, and the strategic use of evidence and communication. The sections below examine how these dynamics manifested across the different system shifts.

### From short-term initiatives with limited scope to long-term, health system–wide transformations

A common shift across countries involved transitioning from short-term, politically expedient health initiatives to longer-term, system-wide reforms rooted in PHC principles. While not specific to PHC per se, this shift was a shared characteristic of the most successful reforms in our sample. It relied on sustained political will and commitment from senior leaders, consistent investment across successive governments, and the ability to articulate and pursue long-term system goals. While several countries in our sample (Egypt, Kazakhstan, Kenya, New Zealand, Thailand, Tunisia, and Uruguay) benefited from high political commitment by senior leaders, only some of those—notably Kazakhstan, Thailand, Uruguay, and New Zealand (for over two decades)—were able to initiate and sustain system-wide PHC reforms.

Politically, these shifts required persuading senior leaders and key interest groups to prioritize comprehensive PHC reforms over short-term, more visible expansions of curative care. Because PHC-oriented reforms channel resources into preventive and promotive services, they often yield limited short-term political gains compared to hospital construction or expansion of disease-specific programs. Leaders’ political incentives, citizens’ demand for tangible near-term benefits, and donors’ pressure for measurable outputs often combined to undermine reform momentum across political cycles.

Reform proponents in various countries employed distinct strategies to navigate these dynamics. They secured high-level political endorsements through persistent mobilization, advocacy, and by leveraging agenda-setting actions by influential non-state actors—such as the World Bank, United Nations agencies, and United States Agency for International Development in the DRC, Egypt, and Kenya; labor unions and social movements in Uruguay; and the Ministry of Public Health (MOPH) leaders in Thailand, whose commitment to universal PHC coverage anchored reform momentum. Countries also leveraged low-veto political environments and centralized decision-making following critical junctures—for example, significant electoral victories in Thailand and Uruguay that produced parliamentary majorities prior to reform adoption, and systemic political transitions in the DRC, Kazakhstan, and Tunisia. Many countries also strategically leveraged macroeconomic conditions. While recessions posed major challenges in Kazakhstan, Thailand, and Uruguay, they also created political space for redistributive reforms, whereas periods of economic growth and fiscal expansion created opportunities to scale PHC investments and sustain reforms over time. For instance, Thailand’s fiscal growth after the Asian Financial Crisis, Uruguay’s use of tax reforms postrecession to increase fiscal space, and Kazakhstan’s rapid growth following the financial crisis of 2008, all generated momentum for PHC investment. Leaders in the DRC, Kazakhstan, New Zealand, Thailand, Tunisia, and Uruguay framed PHC reforms to align with national priorities and broader societal values, positioning them within policy agendas already prioritized by senior political leadership. These countries also institutionalized PHC policies through constitutional changes, legislation, and governance reforms (discussed later), which safeguarded the reforms from political turnover, albeit with mixed results.

### From centralized control to devolved multilevel governance

A significant shift characterizing many PHC reforms in the countries studied involved transitioning from centralized control toward devolved multilevel governance. This shift aimed to empower lower levels of governance with greater roles in decision-making, reform design, resource allocation, implementation, and monitoring and evaluation. It often required aligning national and subnational actors through supportive legislation and regulatory frameworks, reallocating budgets from central to subnational administrations, and redefining or expanding the roles and authority of local administrators, bureaucrats, and politicians, sometimes through the creation of new institutions. New Zealand established new decentralized District Health Boards and Primary Health Organizations. Thailand devolved the MOPH controlled subdistrict health centers to the locally elected Provincial Administrative Office. Kenya decentralized health to county governments, and the DRC’s Provincial Health Division and Health Inspectorates decentralized authority to provinces in line with their broader national governance reforms. While Kazakhstan maintained centralized decision-making authority for health reforms, it empowered regional administrations (akimats) to lead context-specific implementation.

This shift from centralized to devolved governance redistributed authority and power across national, subnational, and local levels, generating distinct political economy challenges. Newly created and decentralized administrations generally supported the change, whereas central government institutions often resisted ceding control or failed to allocate sufficient resources to decentralized entities, provoking vertical and horizontal power struggles and competition for influence and resources. Debates centered around financial autonomy, budget allocations, and the scope of subnational responsibilities. Outcomes also varied depending on the political importance of particular subnational regions to national leaders and the degree of political alignment between national and subnational governments, as well as the strength of local leadership and administrative capacity. In the DRC and Kenya, politically aligned or electorally significant counties and provinces received more resources and were perceived to implement reforms more successfully. In the DRC, the central government has at times reported that subnational authorities refused to finance health services, meet accountability requirements, or implement national directives. Kenyan counties frequently accused the central government of delaying or reducing budget allocations, placing primary-care services in financial distress. Similarly, in New Zealand, rural districts serving marginalized populations often exhibited weaker implementation than better-resourced counterparts.

To manage these political economy dynamics, reformers adopted multiple strategic approaches. Countries like the DRC, Kazakhstan, Kenya, and Thailand enacted legal frameworks or constitutional provisions to mandate devolution, embedding reforms within structures resilient to political turnover and reinforcing accountability to broader constituencies. The new institutions in the DRC, Kenya, New Zealand, and Thailand formalized these mandates and supported their operationalization, albeit with varied success. To encourage alignment of subnational entities with national PHC objectives, the DRC and Kazakhstan used conditional resource transfers as incentives. Kazakhstan and Kenya also invested in building local leadership capacities to reduce resource competition and enhance effectiveness. Finally, at the beginning of its reforms, New Zealand pursued sequenced decentralization, systematically managing resistance and attempting smoother power transitions.

### From hospital-centric resource allocation to strategic reallocations favoring primary care

The reforms involved a significant shift in how resources were distributed within health systems—specifically, by increasing financial and human resources for PHC. In many contexts this implied fewer resources for hospitals. Additionally, several reforms expanded the role of primary-care providers and introduced gatekeeping (mandatory referrals to access hospital services). This shift—implemented most prominently in Kazakhstan, New Zealand, Thailand, and Uruguay, and attempted to varying extents in Egypt, Kenya, and Tunisia—sought to strengthen PHC as the system’s foundation and improve health-system efficiency and equity by enhancing accessibility and responsiveness at the primary-care level, while allowing hospitals to focus on specialized services.

The shift generated predictable political economy frictions. Entrenched medical hierarchies—particularly specialist groups and hospital associations—resisted potential losses of resources, patients, and authority. Contested budgetary priorities and reallocations intensified political debates, requiring reformers to demonstrate the value of investing in primary care, particularly its role in improving equitable access for rural and low-income populations, to political leaders, interest groups, and the public. Patients and communities accustomed to hospital-based care often resisted the move toward greater reliance on primary-care services. Patients and communities long accustomed to hospital-based care also resisted the shift toward increased reliance on primary-care services.

To navigate these dynamics, reformers drew on several strategies. Kazakhstan, Thailand, and Uruguay leveraged macroeconomic growth to expand total health budgets and allocate additional resources for PHC. In New Zealand, objections from providers to capitation payments reforms were mitigated by overall increases in PHC funding. Thailand provided transitional budget support to some hospitals in the initial phases of reform, reducing institutional resistance and smoothing the shift toward a PHC-oriented system. Reformers in the DRC, Kazakhstan, New Zealand, Thailand, and Uruguay also used data-driven narratives highlighting the cost-effectiveness and equity benefits of PHC to build support among stakeholders and the public. Finally, in Kazakhstan, granting managerial and fiscal autonomy to rural hospital managers allowed local leaders to reallocate resources across providers within multidisciplinary PHC teams, adjust staffing and service organization, and strengthen coordination between primary-care facilities and referral hospitals.

### From physician-dominated care to multidisciplinary teams with non-physician providers

Another key shift was from physician-dominated service delivery models to collaborative, multidisciplinary teams, including greater reliance on non-physician providers such as nurses and community health workers, most prominently in Dominica, the DRC, Egypt, Kazakhstan, Kenya, New Zealand, Thailand, and Tunisia. This shift aimed to enhance access to and continuity of care, better align services with PHC principles of comprehensive and community-based care, and address persistent physician shortages.

The shift to multidisciplinary teams generated political economy tensions around professional hierarchies and territories, role redefinitions, and scope of practice. Physicians often resisted, concerned about losing patients, budgets, incomes, and clinical authority. While most non-physician providers supported this shift, some resisted increased workloads and inadequate remuneration. Both physicians and non-physicians frequently resisted team-based decision-making and shared earnings. Communities accustomed to physician-led care were also reluctant to accept services from non-physician providers.

Reformers employed various strategies to manage these dynamics. Kazakhstan engaged physicians through structured dialogue facilitated by the National Association for PHC and conducted interprofessional training sessions to build acceptance of multidisciplinary teams and ease role redefinitions. At the micro level, facility managers fostered distributed leadership across district hospitals and subdistrict health centers, encouraging innovation and ensuring full PHC coverage; national investments in training across all cadres and strong rural-retention policies underpinned this approach. Thailand leveraged its long-standing equity agenda and commitment by public health-oriented physician leaders in government. It invested in training and education of all cadres of the health workforce with strong policies focused on mandatory rural service, which improved retention of health workers in underserved areas. Village health volunteers and civil society organizations (including patient groups) reinforced acceptance through peer support and community engagement. In Tunisia, reformers had some early success by bringing physician associations in joint working groups to co-design family practice models and introduce family medicine as a specialty in medical colleges. Dominica and Egypt emphasized empowering community health workers by embedding them within communities and providing targeted training to build competencies and trust among both patients and providers. Finally, using early adopters before scaling helped demonstrate effectiveness and reduce resistance in the DRC, Kazakhstan, and Kenya.

### From siloed disease-focused services to integrated models of comprehensive care

PHC reforms sought to move from siloed, disease-specific services toward integrated models of comprehensive care. Almost all the countries in our sample attempted this shift, some with more success than others. This shift aimed to strengthen integration across levels of care within the health system, linking preventive, promotive, curative, and rehabilitative services and improving coordination between primary-care providers, multidisciplinary teams, and referral hospitals. The shift to integrated care generated several political economy challenges. Institutional resistance emerged as reformers sought to reorganize services and overcome fragmentation across levels of care. For example, in Kenya and Egypt, efforts to link primary-care facilities more closely with referral hospitals required new coordination arrangements that some providers initially resisted, as these changes altered established referral practices and professional hierarchies. Specialists and physicians accustomed to disease-focused, episodic care often resisted reforms that threatened established clinical practices or income streams. Conversely, community-based providers and nongovernmental organizations often supported these changes, as integrated models expanded their roles in service delivery and community engagement.

Reform actors employed various strategies to overcome these challenges. New Zealand, Thailand, and Uruguay established clearly defined roles, robust referral mechanisms, and stronger linkages across primary, secondary, and tertiary care levels. Thailand used Contracting Units for Primary Care (CUPs) as fund holders through contractual arrangements with the National Health Security Office (NHSO), effectively breaking down silos and incentivizing integration. Kazakhstan, New Zealand, and, in pilot settings in Kenya, implemented multidisciplinary teams comprising physicians and non-physician providers to foster collaborative, integrated care. Reformers also invested in strategic communication and change-management initiatives to shift institutional mindsets and reduce “turf”-driven resistance. In Kazakhstan, a nongovernmental organization with national PHC experts brokered dialogue among regional governments, beneficiaries, and local stakeholders to build support for the implementation of multidisciplinary team-based PHC. Additionally, reforms in Kazakhstan, New Zealand, Thailand, and Uruguay adjusted provider incentives to encourage preventive and promotive care, aligning financial interests with integrated service delivery goals (discussed below). These countries also used phased rollouts to pilot integration models, address coordination challenges, and manage resistance from entrenched service structures. However, countries such as Egypt and Tunisia achieved only limited success due to weak alignment of provider incentives with integrated care and limited strategies to address fragmentation—particularly between public and private sectors (discussed below).

### From peripheral, minimally regulated private sectors to their integration, with actively state-stewarded participation

A common shift (notably in New Zealand, Thailand, and Uruguay) was from viewing private providers as peripheral or minimally regulated actors to actively integrating and stewarding them within national PHC frameworks. Through different types of contractual agreements and policies, the intent was to align private sector contributions with public health and PHC goals, expand service coverage, and ensure quality and equity across the health system.

Powerful private sector providers resisted stricter quality and accountability standards, private insurers opposed mandatory benefits packages that threatened revenues, and some stakeholders raised concerns about quality and incentive alignment, objecting to private sector participation in publicly financed systems. In some cases, reform proponents sought to reorient the health system toward greater focus on equity but faced opposition from private primary-care providers whose profit opportunities were not in areas of greatest health need.

Reformers adopted various strategies to navigate these dynamics. In Kazakhstan, New Zealand, Thailand, and Uruguay, reformers strategically empaneled private providers into government-financed PHC programs and regulated them through formal mechanisms like explicit empanelment criteria, contracts, and payment systems, coupled with service mandates to deliver specified PHC services and follow referral guidelines. Policy framing, especially in New Zealand and Thailand, emphasized public–private collaboration rather than competition, seeking to make both sectors more willing to engage with each other. In New Zealand, the combination of a large public hospital sector and a large private primary-care sector meant that such public–private collaboration was grounded in institutional integration to ensure care continuity and integrated care. In Thailand, the NHSO’s equal treatment of public and private PHC providers through similar terms, conditions, and payment rates made the reform transition smoother, while fraud and false claims by contracted private providers were countered by an auditing system.

### From passive input-based budget allocations and provider payments to strategic purchasing

Another important shift was from traditional input-based financing or fee-for-service payments toward strategic purchasing mechanisms, including instituting purchaser–provider splits and the introduction of blended payment models with salaries, capitation, and performance-based incentives. Seen most prominently in Kazakhstan, New Zealand, Thailand, and Uruguay, this shift sought to align provider behavior with PHC goals of disease prevention and population well-being, while incentivizing quality, accountability, and efficiency.

Transitioning to these forms of strategic purchasing, with different service and cost-related incentives, sparked significant resistance among providers accustomed to fee-for-service models—which rewards volume and stimulates supplier-induced demand and cost escalation—and among those newly subject to stricter performance and accountability standards imposed by purchasers. Smaller purchasers resisted losing market power, since this shift often consolidated several fragmented government and private insurance programs. For example, the creation of purchaser–provider splits and new purchasing organizations such as New Zealand’s District Health Boards, Thailand’s NHSO, and Uruguay’s Fondo Nacional de Salud (National Health Fund) shifted financial authority away from ministries of health, leaving them responsible primarily for providing or overseeing service delivery, and in some cases provoking resistance from political leaders and bureaucrats accustomed to holding both purchasing and service delivery roles.

Reform strategies varied. Kazakhstan, New Zealand, Thailand, and Uruguay leveraged the state’s monopsonistic purchasing power to overcome provider opposition and negotiate capitation-based payments and introduce performance incentives linked to quality standards. Gradual implementation of new payment rules and quality benchmarks helped manage resistance and facilitated smoother transitions. Each of these countries engaged physicians through formal committees to set standards of care quality, service packages, and care pathways. In Thailand and Uruguay, separate purchasing institutions were established through legislation, granting clear mandates and distinct accountability vis-à-vis ministries of health. In both countries, the ministries of health played key roles in governing these purchasing institutions to secure their support. In Thailand, the multistakeholder governance of the Universal Health Coverage Scheme (UCS), with the MOPH serving as one of 30 ex officio board members under the chairmanship of the Ministry of Health, helped ensure transparency and accountability.

### From perceiving citizens as passive recipients of care to building active community engagement

Across all countries in our sample—albeit with varying degrees of success—reforms sought to move from viewing citizens as passive recipients of care toward meaningful community participation, including trust-building between health systems and the populations they serve. The aim was to challenge entrenched preferences for hospital-based, physician-led care, strengthen confidence in community-based services, and create participatory platforms that enabled communities to influence health policy and service delivery.

These shifts generated notable political economy tensions. Political leaders and bureaucrats often resisted ceding control or exposure to greater scrutiny. A stronger community voice frequently translated into demands for more transparent allocation of resources, improved responsiveness, and redress of local grievances—pressures that threatened established patronage networks and bureaucratic discretion. Providers, particularly physicians and facility managers, expressed skepticism or opposed expanded patient and community decision-making, seeing it as encroaching on professional autonomy. Where medical lobbies were strong or provider markets fragmented, these tensions were especially pronounced. Local capacity to support genuine community engagement also varied widely: differences in literacy, civil society strength, and prior experience with participatory governance shaped what was feasible. In settings lacking robust civic organizations or where social hierarchies constrained open dialogue, engagement risked becoming tokenistic, with community platforms used to legitimize predetermined decisions rather than to shift power relations.

Reformers employed several strategies to manage these dynamics. Kazakhstan prioritized structured consultations with community representatives to identify priority health needs, monitor service quality, and propose improvements to PHC service design. These efforts helped build trust and reshape public attitudes toward PHC and stimulated greater interest among local and regional governments in implementing multidisciplinary team-based PHC. Tunisia initiated inclusive societal dialogues for health, fostering public discourse on health reform postdemocratization in 2011, though these efforts waned due to political instability. Uruguay institutionalized community representation within governance structures, such as Junta Nacional de Salud (National Health Board), while the DRC relied on local health committees (Comités de Santé) to link health facilities with communities. Thailand’s National Health Assembly provided a national forum for inclusive dialogue, while mandatory nationwide annual public hearings redressed problems. Civil society representation in the governance of the UCS ensures that citizen voices are heard and increases the likelihood that challenges are addressed. In parallel, Kazakhstan, Thailand, and Uruguay incrementally expanded coverage and benefits toward PHC, avoiding reductions in coverage for existing beneficiaries and, thereby, enhancing public acceptance of and satisfaction with the reforms. Economic growth in these countries (discussed above) facilitated these expansions.

### From ad hoc evaluation to embedded learning and accountability

A notable transition, especially in Kazakhstan, Thailand, and Uruguay, was toward embedding continuous learning, evaluation, and accountability within reform processes, including systematic data collection and analysis of patient experience. The aim was to keep reforms responsive to real-world challenges, agile and adaptable over time, and closely aligned with community needs.

Embedding learning and accountability involved navigating credibility challenges: reformers had to persuade skeptical stakeholders and use evidence strategically to sustain political momentum and secure buy-in. Administrators and managers sometimes resisted increased data collection burdens, while political leaders and external actors occasionally opposed evaluations that could show reform shortcomings.

To navigate these dynamics, reformers in Kazakhstan, Thailand, and Uruguay strategically disseminated favorable evaluation findings domestically and internationally to bolster legitimacy and attract further support for their PHC reforms. They leveraged evidence to maintain political support and counter opposition narratives. Patient experience data were shared with political leaders and bureaucrats to demonstrate popular support and reduce resistance. In Thailand, the reform’s tangible improvements in service delivery and financial risk protection generated popular support, which helped sustain the reform through multiple changes in regime and political leadership. In Kazakhstan, positive patient experience data helped gain the support of local mayors (akims) and bureaucrats for the reform. More broadly, showcasing domestic achievements against international benchmarks and earning peer recognition reinforced a culture of ongoing learning and continuous improvement of the reforms.

### From externally driven changes to local ownership for reforms

A final transition involved moving from externally imposed reforms driven by international donors and actors to reforms characterized by local ownership and alignment with domestic priorities and values. This approach emphasized national sovereignty and long-term sustainability, increasing the likelihood that reform designs would resonate with local stakeholders.

This shift generated several complex dynamics. Where reforms were externally driven, domestic actors often demonstrated limited ownership, jeopardizing the sustainability of initiatives. Power imbalances between donors and domestic stakeholders shaped reform implementation. Additionally, the politics of ideas played a crucial role—externally imposed reforms based on international templates frequently clashed with local policy legacies, cultural norms, and institutional structures, creating significant friction and resistance.

In response, reformers grounded their initiatives in local values, institutional histories, and policy legacies, such as Thailand’s MOPH commitment to universal coverage through the district health system, Uruguay’s traditions of labor rights and social security, the DRC’s political decentralization, and New Zealand’s Treaty of Waitangi. They invested in domestic technical capacity within institutions and among individual stakeholders to strengthen design and implementation capabilities, as seen in Kazakhstan and Thailand. Collaboration with external actors evolved into partnerships based on reciprocal knowledge exchange rather than unilateral direction. Finally, countries such as Kazakhstan, New Zealand, Thailand, and Uruguay prioritized domestic financing for their reforms, reducing reliance (or not relying at all) on donor funds to enhance autonomy and reform sustainability.

## Discussion

This study analyzes how nine countries—DRC, Dominica, Egypt, Kazakhstan, Kenya, New Zealand, Thailand, Tunisia, and Uruguay—initiated, implemented, and sustained (to varying degrees) PHC-oriented reforms. We analyzed patterns in the directions of change, identified 10 key health-system shifts, and synthesized the political economy dynamics each shift faced and the strategies that reformers used to navigate them. The shifts were often resisted by entrenched interests and required context-specific, deliberate strategies. While it is well recognized that health reforms are inherently political, this study shows how political economy dynamics shape the implementation of PHC-oriented reforms and reform actors use different strategies to adapt in practice. Rather than treating opposing interest groups as monolithic, we emphasize within-group heterogeneity and argue for coalition strategies that identify and align groups whose incentives can be made congruent with PHC while minimizing resistance. The findings underscore the value of anticipating political economy dynamics in the design and implementation of PHC-oriented reforms.

Although common patterns emerged across the country cases, there were also significant differences in the scope, sequencing, and institutional context of reforms. Countries varied in the breadth and depth of PHC-oriented reforms, the strength of state institutions responsible for implementation, and the fiscal space available to support reforms. These contextual differences shaped both the political economy dynamics encountered and the strategies available to reformers. While the present study focuses on identifying cross-cutting patterns across diverse settings, future comparative work could examine more systematically how variation in institutional capacity, political structures, reform design, and economic conditions influences the implementation and sustainability of PHC-oriented reforms.

The 10 shifts depict fundamental reconfigurations of health systems toward PHC. Most countries used multiple shifts; notably, those that have been able to sustain and strengthen their PHC-oriented reforms over time (Kazakhstan, New Zealand, Thailand, and Uruguay) observed all 10 shifts in some form across different stages of their reforms, with the shifts often reinforcing one another. This pattern aligns with evidence that successful health reforms involve coherent changes across several policy levers, such as financing, organization of the delivery system, providers’ payments, community engagement, and governance (Roberts et al. 2004, Atun et al. 2015, Sparkes et al. 2019, Yip et al. 2023, WHO 2024).

Across shifts, several political economy dynamics recurred. Redistributive features of PHC-oriented reforms often threatened vested interests—physicians defending their scopes of practice, autonomy, and incomes; hospitals and specialists wary of losing patient volumes and revenues; or private providers and insurers resisting regulation. Political leaders were sometimes reluctant to champion reforms that promised limited immediate, visible payoffs, while citizens, accustomed to hospital-centric models, were skeptical of community-based, non-physician providers or preventive services. Decentralization added tensions between central government demands for uniformity and control versus subnational demands for autonomy, while uneven local administrative capacity produced variable implementation and fueled political bargaining. Interactions between domestic agendas and external actors—where donor priorities sometimes clashed with local institutional legacies—further complicated reform trajectories.

The most common political economy dynamic was physician opposition to multiple shifts such as resource reallocation from hospitals to PHC, expansion of non-physician roles and multidisciplinary teams, changes to provider payment mechanisms, integrated comprehensive care, stronger stewardship of the private sector, enhanced community engagement, accountable governance, and more broadly, long-term systemic transformation.

A second prominent political economy dynamic was resistance from leaders, administrators, and bureaucrats to shifts that threatened the status quo, particularly strategic purchasing (especially from fee for service toward more closed-end payment), embedded learning and accountability in the health system, and expanded citizen participation. The circumstances that generated such commitment were highly context dependent. PHC advocates played key roles in agenda setting and design but often relied on unpredictable “windows of opportunity.” In New Zealand and Thailand, designs were prepared and negotiated in advance so that, when political windows opened, leaders could move quickly to enactment and early wins. Commitment from senior political leadership was foundational to launching and sustaining reforms, especially when paired with accommodating institutional environments and limited veto points in legislative processes, enabling comprehensive legislation and clear mandates. The circumstances and strategies that generated such commitment were highly context dependent.

Another observation is that, perhaps contrary to what PHC advocates often assume, support for PHC-oriented reforms from citizens and from some service providers (like nurses, social workers, and psychologists) was not automatic. In several countries, significant resistance came from citizens unwilling to accept primary care and community-based services, especially those provided by non-physician personnel, instead of physicians and hospitals. Some primary-care providers also resisted when roles and workload expanded, or payment and accountability mechanisms changed. Professional hierarchies played a role in some of these tensions, including reluctance to work in multidisciplinary teams.

These political economy dynamics are similar to the types of politics identified by Campos and Reich (2019) and in the country case studies based on our study (Ashubwe et al. 2024, Jurgutis et al. 2024, Matheson et al. 2024, Schenck et al. 2024, Tangcharoensathien et al. 2024). For instance, physician opposition could be mapped as a form of interest group politics; opposition (and support) from administrators and bureaucrats as bureaucratic politics; commitment of senior political leaders as leadership politics; and opposition from citizens as beneficiary politics. We also see the category of “budget politics” across different stakeholders; and external actor politics where donors shaped the reform space and ideas (especially in donor dependent contexts). In the country case studies, we identified another category—“organizational politics”—that pertains to interprofessional hierarchies (Ashubwe et al. 2024, Jurgutis et al. 2024, Schenck et al. 2024). While the typology was helpful for the country-level analysis, our intention in this paper is to highlight the nuances of the political economy dynamics and describe the way they may manifest in the context of PHC-oriented reforms.

Reform actors deployed various political strategies: leveraging political authority or economic conditions; brokering stakeholder alignment or transitional compromises; shaping public narratives; and creating or redesigning institutions and incentives. These strategies worked best when sequenced and combined to meet evolving political economy challenges throughout the reform process. Effectiveness, however, was context dependent. Economic growth enabled Kazakhstan, Thailand, and Uruguay to expand PHC budgets, but similar fiscal strategies were less feasible in countries facing limited economic growth. Legal mandates helped where the state could enforce them, whereas weaker regulatory environments struggled. Community engagement thrived where local capacities and participatory traditions existed and were supported by political will to engage but risked being pro forma or symbolic engagement where they did not. Even widely used strategies—gradual implementation or quality-linked payments—had mixed results depending on administrative capacity and stakeholder trust. This underscores that broad principles for navigating political economy tensions are transferable, but success hinges on careful adaptation to political, institutional, and socioeconomic context.

Several policy implications follow. First, countries designing PHC-oriented reforms should assess not only the technical requirements but also the distributional implications of reform—anticipating resistance and planning responses. Second, embedding reforms in reconfigured or new institutions, backed by legislation or durable mandates, enhances their resilience across political cycles. Third, sustained investment in communication, data, and meaningful community engagement is essential for political support and legitimacy, particularly under conditions of democratic contestation, polarization, or fragility. Fourth, implementation should allow flexible, transitional arrangements (e.g. supplemental hospital budgets or phased workforce changes) to ease opposition and enable sustainable long-term shifts. Finally, institutional and individual capacities for political economy analysis and strategic responses should be strengthened through collaborations among researchers, practitioners, policy entrepreneurs, and policymakers, alongside training and resources.

Future research could examine how political strategies are adapted across contexts, especially in countries where PHC reforms coincide with broader health-system transitions. The growing role of digital health, drug, and diagnostic technologies also warrants attention; understanding how these intersect with political economy dynamics—around data governance, cost escalations, provider roles, and citizen engagement—will be critical. Developing practical tools to help countries prospectively understand and account for political economy dynamics in PHC-oriented reforms, particularly in relation to the common shifts identified, appears both useful and warranted.

This study has several limitations. While we drew from both primary and secondary sources, the depth and scope of data varied across countries, potentially influencing the granularity of comparative insights. Although our sample spans all WHO regions, it is not globally representative, and countries differ on state capacities and on socioeconomic, political, and health-system characteristics, limiting comparative inference. Some interviews and FGDs were retrospective, with potential recall bias, particularly where reforms occurred a decade or more ago. While the WHO PHC Operational Framework provided a consistent analytical lens, our categorization of strategies and dynamics inevitably involved subjective interpretation and synthesis.

With carefully sequenced and context-sensitive strategies, reformers have navigated significant political economy challenges to advance more equitable, people-centered health systems. As countries renew commitments to PHC in pursuit of universal health coverage and the Sustainable Development Goals, acknowledging and addressing the political economy of reforms will be essential—not only for effective design but also for inclusive, durable, and sustained implementation.

## Reflexivity statement

Our multicountry team brought diverse positionalities to this study, including those of academics, clinicians, policy analysts, government officials, and staff of international agencies. Several authors were employed by or funded via the WHO during parts of the research. Many country research team members and authors of this paper were directly involved in the PHC reforms we studied here, as policy designers, implementers, or technical advisors, while others were external researchers. These insider/outsider positions shaped access to respondents and documents and may have influenced our interpretation of particular political economy dynamics in this paper. To mitigate bias, we conducted paired coding by investigators with different roles and implemented systematic triangulation of interviews, policy documents, and secondary literature. We acknowledge power and language asymmetries in cross-national qualitative work; to reduce misinterpretation, local researchers led interviews in local languages, translations were cross-checked, and preliminary findings were member checked with selected respondents. These steps do not eliminate positional bias but seek to make its influence more transparent, strengthening the credibility and transferability of our analysis.
